common_name: General Schablikine Tea Rose (Copper-Red Antique Tea Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in fall or late winter in well-drained soil; General Schablikine, introduced in France in 1878, is a vigorous copper-red tea rose long favored in Deep South gardens for its heat tolerance.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil, giving the bushy, free-flowering habit room to spread into a substantial hedge or specimen shrub. Bred by Gilbert Nabonnand in France in 1878, General Schablikine produces richly double, coppery red-orange blooms shaded with cherry-pink that open from long pointed buds into nearly flat, informal flowers carrying the classic tea fragrance. It is one of the toughest old tea roses for Gulf Coast gardens, flowering almost continuously from spring into fall and shrugging off heat and humidity that cause many modern roses to struggle, with notably good resistance to blackspot. Prune lightly after the main spring flush to maintain shape and encourage repeat bloom.

common_name: Madame Berkeley Tea Rose (Salmon-Pink Antique Tea Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in fall in rich, well-drained soil; Madame Berkeley, introduced in France in 1898, bears large salmon-pink blooms and performs reliably through Gulf Coast summer heat.

directions: Plant in full sun in rich, well-drained soil. Madame Berkeley, bred by Pierre Bernaix in France in 1898, bears large, shell-shaped, semi-double blooms in warm salmon-pink with a strong, classic tea fragrance. Like other antique teas, it holds up well through Gulf Coast summer heat and humidity, blooming in flushes from spring to frost with minimal spraying needed. Give it good air circulation to limit fungal disease in humid weather, and deadhead spent blooms to encourage continued flowering.

common_name: Rosette Delizy Tea Rose (Yellow-and-Carmine Antique Tea Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in fall in well-drained soil; Rosette Delizy, introduced in France in the early 1920s, is a compact bicolor tea rose well suited to smaller Gulf Coast beds.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil. Rosette Delizy, bred by Paul Nabonnand in France and introduced in the early 1920s, produces large, full, reflexed blooms with rich yellow centers edged in carmine-pink, an uncommon bicolor among old tea roses. More compact than many teas, rarely exceeding four feet, it suits smaller Gulf Coast gardens while retaining the class's typical heat tolerance and near-continuous bloom from spring to frost. Light, frequent pruning keeps the naturally twiggy growth tidy and encourages fresh flowering wood.

common_name: Adam Tea Rose (Salmon-Apricot Antique Tea-Noisette, also sold as Madame Berard)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in fall, giving them room to develop into a large shrub or short climber; Adam, raised in Reims, France in the 1830s, is regarded by many rosarians as the first Tea rose.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil, giving it space to develop into a large shrub or short climber on a pillar or fence. Raised in Reims, France, in the 1830s and sometimes sold under the synonym Madame Berard, Adam is considered by many rosarians to be the first Tea rose and a direct ancestor of the class, bearing fully double, salmon-pink blooms tinted apricot and buff with a rich tea fragrance. It carries the vigor and heat tolerance typical of the earliest tea roses, thriving in Gulf Coast gardens where modern hybrid teas often falter. Prune mainly to shape and remove old or crowded wood rather than hard pruning, since much of the bloom is carried on mature canes.

common_name: Alexander Hill Gray Tea Rose (Deepening Lemon-Yellow Antique Tea Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in fall in well-drained soil; Alexander Hill Gray, introduced in 1911, is a compact, intensely fragrant lemon-yellow tea rose suited to smaller beds.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil. Alexander Hill Gray, introduced in 1911, is a compact tea rose with large, high-centered, intensely fragrant blooms that open soft lemon-yellow and deepen in color as they age. Its smaller stature, rarely exceeding three feet, makes it useful for borders and beds where taller antique roses would overwhelm the space. Like other tea roses it tolerates Gulf Coast heat and humidity better than modern hybrid teas, though its pale yellow petals can bleach in the most intense summer sun, so light afternoon shade in the hottest climates helps preserve color. Deadhead regularly to prolong the bloom season.

common_name: Gruss an Teplitz Rose (Scarlet-Red China/Bourbon Hybrid Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in fall in average, well-drained soil; Gruss an Teplitz, introduced in Germany in 1897, is an unusually vigorous, heat-tolerant scarlet old rose of mixed China-Bourbon ancestry.

directions: Plant in full sun in average, well-drained soil. Gruss an Teplitz, introduced in Germany in 1897 and bred from China and Bourbon rose parentage, is difficult to pigeonhole taxonomically but is usually grown and sold alongside old China roses. It bears clustered, double, strongly spice-scented scarlet-red blooms that darken with age, flowering in repeated flushes from spring through fall. Notably vigorous and disease-resistant for an antique rose, it tolerates Gulf Coast heat and humidity well and can be grown as a large shrub or trained as a short climber on a fence or pillar. Prune back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering canes.

common_name: Bouquet d'Or Noisette Rose (Coppery-Gold Climbing Noisette)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in fall against a sturdy support; Bouquet d'Or, a 1872 sport of Gloire de Dijon, is a vigorous climbing Noisette bred for Southern heat.

directions: Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade against a fence, pergola, or wall sturdy enough to support its long climbing canes. Bouquet d'Or, a sport of Gloire de Dijon introduced in France in 1872, bears large, double, coppery gold-and-apricot blooms with a rich fruity fragrance, repeating in flushes from spring into fall. Like other Noisettes, it carries good Southern heat tolerance and performs well through Gulf Coast summers, though afternoon shade in the hottest climates helps keep bloom color from fading. Train canes horizontally along supports to maximize flowering along their length, and prune out only dead or weak wood in late winter.

common_name: Solfaterre Noisette Rose (Pale Sulfur-Yellow Climbing Noisette)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in fall against a trellis or fence; Solfaterre, introduced in France in the early 1840s, is a vigorous pale-yellow climbing Noisette well suited to hot, humid summers.

directions: Plant in full sun against a trellis, arbor, or fence, since Solfaterre is a vigorous climber reaching eight feet or more. Bred in France and introduced in the early 1840s, it produces large, very double, pale sulfur-yellow blooms carried in big, lax clusters that repeat through the season with a mild fragrance. As a true Noisette, a class originally developed in Charleston, South Carolina before being refined in France, it is well adapted to hot, humid Gulf Coast summers and resists the blackspot that plagues many modern roses in the region. Allow some older wood to remain when pruning, since flowering is heaviest on two- and three-year-old canes.

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in fall in well-drained soil; Fellemberg, introduced in the 1830s, is a compact, cluster-flowered Noisette sometimes sold as La Belle Marseillaise.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil. Fellemberg, introduced in the 1830s and sometimes offered under the name La Belle Marseillaise, bears large trusses of double, cupped, bright crimson-cerise blooms with a light fragrance, repeating reliably from late spring to frost. More compact than many climbing Noisettes, it can be grown as a large shrub or a modest pillar rose. It shares the class's good heat tolerance and performs well in Gulf Coast gardens, though its thin petals can spot in prolonged wet weather. Deadhead and provide good air circulation to keep foliage healthy through humid summers.

common_name: Natchitoches Noisette Rose (Found Pink Cemetery Noisette)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in fall in average garden soil; Natchitoches Noisette, a found rose rescued from an untended Louisiana cemetery, is exceptionally tough in Deep South heat and humidity.

directions: Plant in full sun to part shade in average garden soil. Natchitoches Noisette is a found rose rescued from a century-old, untended cemetery planting in Natchitoches, Louisiana, and named for the town where it was rediscovered. It produces large, full clusters of light pink blooms opening from cherry-red buds, with a distinctive myrrh-and-pepper fragrance, on a repeat-blooming plant that can be kept as a shrub or allowed to climb to about eight feet. Having survived a century of Deep South heat, humidity, and neglect with no spraying or fertilizing, it is about as reliable a choice as exists for Gulf Coast gardens. Minimal pruning is needed beyond shaping and removing dead wood.

common_name: Gipsy Boy Bourbon Rose (Deep Crimson-Purple Bourbon, also sold as Zigeunerknabe)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in fall in average, well-drained soil; Gipsy Boy, introduced in Germany in 1909 under the name Zigeunerknabe, is a tough, thicket-forming Bourbon tolerant of poor soil.

directions: Plant in full sun to light shade in average, well-drained soil. Gipsy Boy, also sold under its original German name Zigeunerknabe, was introduced in 1909 and bears medium, double, deep crimson-purple blooms that fade toward maroon, with primrose-yellow stamens and a strong fragrance. It blooms mainly in a single large flush in late spring with some scattered repeat, and its arching, thicket-forming canes make it useful as an informal hedge or large specimen shrub. More cold-hardy than many Bourbons and notably tolerant of poor soil, it also holds up reasonably well to Gulf Coast heat, though its once-blooming habit concentrates the display earlier in the season than true repeat Bourbons. Prune immediately after flowering to shape without removing next year's wood.

common_name: Great Western Bourbon Rose (Quartered Mauve-Purple Antique Bourbon)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in fall in fertile, well-drained soil; Great Western, introduced around 1840, is a deep mauve-purple Bourbon with strong old-rose fragrance.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil. Great Western, bred by Jean Laffay in France and introduced around 1840, bears large, full, quartered blooms in deep mauve-purple to purplish-maroon shades against dark green foliage, with a strong old-rose fragrance. It flowers heavily in a late-spring-to-summer flush with lighter repeat bloom later in the season. Sometimes classed as a hybrid Bourbon for its unusually dark, saturated color, it tolerates Gulf Coast heat reasonably well but benefits from afternoon shade in the hottest climates to prevent the dark petals from scorching. Remove only dead or crossing wood in late winter to preserve the arching habit.

common_name: Coquette des Blanches Bourbon Rose (Blush-White Repeat-Blooming Bourbon)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in fall in well-drained soil; Coquette des Blanches, introduced in France in 1871, is an unusually disease-resistant, cold-hardy white Bourbon.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil. Coquette des Blanches, bred by François Lacharme in France in 1871, produces cupped, double, white blooms with a faint blush-pink flush at the center and a light, sweet fragrance, repeating in flushes from late spring to fall. It is notably more disease-resistant and cold-hardy than many Bourbons, and its vigorous, semi-climbing growth suits a pillar, fence, or large shrub border. In Gulf Coast gardens it benefits from good air circulation, since the pale petals can spot in prolonged humid weather, but it generally performs well through summer heat. Deadhead spent blooms to encourage the next flush.

common_name: Schneezwerg Rugosa Rose (White Semi-Double Hybrid Rugosa, Snow Dwarf)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in fall in well-drained soil; Schneezwerg (Snow Dwarf), bred in Germany around 1911, is a cold-hardy hybrid Rugosa that is more heat-sensitive than modern Gulf Coast shrub roses.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil. Schneezwerg, German for 'Snow Dwarf' and bred by Peter Lambert around 1911, is a hybrid Rugosa bearing flat, semi-double, fragrant white blooms with golden stamens, followed by showy orange-red hips, on a dense, bushy, wrinkle-leaved plant. It flowers in repeated flushes from late spring into fall and shows outstanding disease resistance in cooler climates. Rugosa hybrids are bred primarily for cold-hardiness rather than heat tolerance, and in humid Gulf Coast gardens they are more prone to stress and decline than further north, so site this rose with excellent drainage and reserve it for the milder, drier edges of its range rather than the hottest coastal gardens. Avoid heavy mulch against the crown and skip fungicide sprays, which rugosas tend to resent.

common_name: Pink Grootendorst Rugosa Rose (Fringed Carnation-Flowered Hybrid Rugosa)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in fall in well-drained soil; Pink Grootendorst, a 1923 Dutch sport of F.J. Grootendorst, has fringed, carnation-like pink blooms and the salt and wind tolerance typical of rugosa hybrids.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, even sandy soil. Pink Grootendorst, a 1923 Dutch sport of F.J. Grootendorst, bears dense clusters of small, clear pink, double blooms with distinctively fringed, carnation-like petal edges, repeating from late spring to frost. Like other Rugosa hybrids it tolerates salt spray, wind, and poor soil remarkably well, making it useful for exposed plantings. It is bred foremost for cold hardiness, and gardeners in the hottest, most humid parts of the Gulf Coast often see more stress and reduced vigor than it shows farther north, so give it a well-drained site and good air movement. Deadhead regularly to keep the plant tidy, since the fringed petals do not always drop cleanly.

common_name: Linda Campbell Rugosa Rose (Clustered True-Red Hybrid Rugosa)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in fall in well-drained soil; Linda Campbell is a vigorous hybrid Rugosa valued for clustered true-red blooms and relatively better warm-climate performance than many rugosas.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil. Linda Campbell is a vigorous hybrid Rugosa shrub rose bearing large clusters of semi-double, true red blooms with little fragrance, repeating reliably through the growing season. It is more tolerant of varied conditions than many rugosas and is often cited as one of the better choices in the class for warmer gardens, able to be grown as a large shrub, informal hedge, or trained on a support as a short climber. Even so, like other rugosas it can show more disease and heat stress in the most humid Gulf Coast summers than it does in drier or cooler climates, so plant with good air circulation and avoid heavy, poorly drained soils. Minimal pruning beyond removing dead wood is needed.

common_name: Moje Hammarberg Rugosa Rose (Violet-Crimson Fragrant Hybrid Rugosa)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in fall in well-drained soil; Moje Hammarberg, discovered in Sweden in 1931, is an intensely fragrant violet-crimson hybrid Rugosa best suited to cooler, drier climates.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil. Moje Hammarberg, discovered by Mauritz Hammarberg in Sweden in 1931, is a hybrid Rugosa bearing large, double, violet-crimson blooms with an intense, old-rose fragrance, notable for producing both flowers and showy hips simultaneously in late summer. It repeats well through the season and shows strong disease resistance in its preferred cooler, drier climates. As with other rugosas, expect more stress and less vigor in the hot, humid Gulf Coast than in cooler regions; it performs best there in well-drained soil with good air movement, and is better suited to the milder edges of its range than to the hottest coastal gardens. Prune lightly, removing only dead or weak canes.

common_name: Scabrosa Rugosa Rose (Large Single Magenta-Pink Hybrid Rugosa)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in fall in well-drained soil; Scabrosa is an extremely cold-hardy, drought-tolerant hybrid Rugosa grown for large single mauve-pink blooms and oversized hips.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil. Scabrosa is a hybrid Rugosa bearing extra-large single to semi-double magenta-mauve-pink blooms with golden stamens, followed by unusually large, tomato-like orange-red hips that persist into winter. It blooms continuously through summer and is exceptionally cold-hardy and drought-tolerant once established. Like other rugosas it is bred chiefly for cold climates, and gardeners in the hottest, most humid parts of the Gulf Coast often see reduced vigor and more disease pressure than in cooler regions, so give it full sun, sharp drainage, and good air circulation, and consider it primarily for the cooler, drier margins of the region. Avoid rich, wet soils, which rugosas tolerate poorly.
